title: US Democrats Win Congress With an Affordability Promise, but Can They Lower Prices?
shortdescription: Democrats have won control of Congress promising relief from high food, fuel and healthcare costs. But President Trump's veto power and economic pressures could limit what they achieve.
author: Macro Anton

content.content: /images/food fuel.webp

The rising cost of everyday essentials has become one of America's biggest economic and political challenges, and the Democrats' sweeping victories in the November 3 midterm elections have placed the issue at the centre of the next phase of government. With control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, Democrats are preparing to pursue a new affordability agenda covering groceries, fuel, healthcare, housing and taxes. Their election success was driven partly by frustration over household expenses, but winning congressional majorities does not automatically give the party the power to reduce prices. President Donald Trump remains in the White House, global energy markets remain unstable and the incoming Congress will have to negotiate its way through significant political and economic constraints.

The scale of the political message was reflected in voter surveys. The Associated Press's election survey of roughly 100,000 voters found that about nine in ten considered the cost of living a major or crucial factor in their decision, while approximately two-thirds believed Trump's policies had contributed to inflation. High energy costs, import tariffs and concerns about healthcare expenses featured prominently in the election debate. Democrats benefited from that dissatisfaction, but Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer acknowledged that many voters were still sceptical of his party. The incoming leadership now faces pressure to turn an electoral victory into policies that make a measurable difference to household budgets.

The economic picture is more complicated than a simple story of rising inflation. Overall consumer prices were 3.7% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier, according to figures reported by the Associated Press. The US Department of Agriculture's September data showed food prices rising 2.5% year over year, while grocery prices increased 1.8%. Restaurant and other food-service prices rose 3.5%. Although grocery inflation was comparatively moderate, households continue to pay prices that have accumulated over several years of increases. Slower inflation means prices are rising more slowly; it does not necessarily mean supermarket bills are returning to earlier levels.
Food Prices: Competition, Tariffs and Household Support

Groceries are likely to be one of the first areas where Democrats seek policy changes. The party's proposed affordability agenda includes rolling back selected Trump-era import tariffs, supporting smaller food producers and encouraging greater competition in the food marketplace. Democrats argue that reducing trade costs and challenging anti-competitive practices could help ease pressure on consumers. The New Democrat Coalition has also proposed stronger consumer protections and measures aimed at improving choice in essential goods markets.

Tariffs are a particularly important part of the debate because import taxes can increase the cost of products and materials brought into the United States. Businesses may absorb part of the additional expense, but some costs can be passed on to retailers and consumers. Democrats have promised to challenge Trump's trade policies and restore a greater congressional role in tariff decisions. However, the president retains considerable authority over trade policy under existing laws, meaning a new congressional majority cannot simply reverse every tariff through an immediate vote. Any major legislative change could face a presidential veto or require negotiations with Republicans.

Some Democrats have also considered more direct approaches to grocery prices, including proposals targeting large food retailers and encouraging voluntary price limits on selected products. These ideas remain debated rather than agreed national policy. Economists have warned that broad price controls can create supply problems if retailers and producers cannot cover their costs. For that reason, increasing competition, improving supply chains and supporting smaller producers may prove more politically practical than attempting to impose nationwide price caps.
Fuel Prices: A Problem Congress Cannot Solve Alone

Energy costs present a more immediate challenge. The national average price of regular gasoline stood at approximately $4.12 per gallon on November 4, according to AAA data. Fuel prices had reached unusually high levels during the autumn, with September's monthly average at $4.33 per gallon. The prolonged conflict involving Iran has disrupted energy-market expectations and increased uncertainty around shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies. Higher crude prices have affected not only motorists but also businesses facing increased transportation, shipping and production costs.

Democrats may attempt to use congressional powers to influence the administration's approach to the conflict. Reuters reported that the incoming majority could attach conditions to government spending, delay confirmations of officials and pursue war-related resolutions to increase pressure for a diplomatic agreement and secure the Strait of Hormuz. Such moves could give Congress greater influence over the administration's decisions, but they cannot guarantee an immediate reduction in petrol prices. Even a de-escalation of the conflict would not necessarily restore global energy shipments immediately or bring crude prices down to previous levels.

The Democrats are also expected to focus on domestic electricity costs. Their proposed priorities include strengthening consumer protections, reviewing the financial impact of data-centre construction on electricity bills and potentially restoring or extending certain wind, solar and clean-manufacturing tax credits. The rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure has increased demand for electricity, raising questions about who should pay for new power-generation and grid investments. More scrutiny of utility spending could help protect households from unfair cost increases, although new energy infrastructure and regulatory changes generally take time to deliver savings.
Taxes: Potential Relief for Families and Workers

Tax policy offers Democrats another route to provide financial support. One of their priorities is restoring more generous Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired at the end of 2025. These subsidies helped eligible households purchase health insurance through federal and state marketplaces. Their restoration could lower monthly insurance costs for qualifying consumers, although it would not directly reduce grocery or petrol prices. Democrats have also discussed reversing Republican Medicaid cuts and expanding access to affordable healthcare.

The party is also considering expanding the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit, which could provide additional support to families and lower-income workers. The Tax Foundation notes that one proposal could increase the basic Child Tax Credit from $2,200 per child in 2026 to $3,000 or more in 2027. Democrats may also seek to increase support for workers without children through the Earned Income Tax Credit. These measures could improve disposable income for eligible households, but their implementation would depend on legislation, funding decisions and negotiations with the White House.

To finance some of these proposals, Democratic lawmakers are considering higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations. Incoming Senate Finance Committee Chair Ron Wyden has indicated that his agenda will focus on requiring the wealthiest households and businesses to contribute more, alongside healthcare reform and changes to trade policy. Proposals include raising the federal corporate tax rate from its current 21% level and revisiting taxation of high-income individuals. However, these measures remain policy proposals, not enacted changes. Business groups may argue that higher corporate taxes could discourage investment or affect hiring, while supporters say additional revenue could help fund household support and public services.
The Political Limits on Delivering Relief

Despite the new congressional majority, Democrats will not have unlimited legislative power. The incoming Congress is scheduled to begin on January 3, 2027, leaving the existing Republican-controlled Congress in place during the remaining weeks of 2026. Even after Democrats take over, President Trump retains the power to veto legislation. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, a threshold Democrats are not expected to reach. Most ordinary Senate legislation also faces the possibility of a filibuster, which generally requires 60 votes to end debate. A Democratic majority of at least 54 senators therefore does not automatically guarantee that major proposals can become law.

However, Democrats will have significant influence over the congressional budget process, committee investigations and government funding. Reuters reported that their control of spending legislation and the federal borrowing process could give them leverage in negotiations with the Trump administration, particularly over healthcare subsidies and economic policy. They can also use congressional hearings to examine how tariffs, energy decisions and regulatory changes affect consumers and businesses. Even when legislation is blocked, such oversight can shape public debate and put pressure on the administration to reconsider particular policies.

The larger challenge is that not all cost-of-living pressures originate in Washington. Food prices depend on agricultural production, weather, transportation and international supply chains. Fuel prices are heavily influenced by global oil supply, geopolitical developments and refining capacity. Healthcare and housing costs involve complex systems of insurers, providers, developers, state governments and private businesses. Congress can influence these areas through taxes, subsidies, regulations and spending, but it cannot simply order market prices to fall.

For businesses, the shift in congressional control could bring changes in trade policy, corporate taxation, energy regulation and government spending priorities. Import-dependent companies may welcome the possibility of lower tariffs, while some energy and technology businesses could face greater scrutiny over subsidies, emissions rules and electricity consumption. Investors will also be watching whether political negotiations produce stable policy conditions or create further uncertainty around federal spending and taxation.

The Democrats' election victory has therefore created an opportunity to reshape economic policy, but the impact on household finances will depend on what the party can negotiate and implement. Restoring healthcare subsidies, expanding family tax credits and reducing selected trade costs could provide tangible support. Greater energy oversight and pressure for an agreement over Iran could also help address some of the forces behind rising fuel bills. Yet substantial and lasting reductions in the cost of living are unlikely to arrive immediately when the new Congress takes office.

The central test for Hakeem Jeffries, Chuck Schumer and their colleagues will be whether they can move beyond broad affordability promises and agree on legislation that produces measurable benefits. Voters have made clear that food, fuel, healthcare and household expenses matter more than political messaging alone. Democrats now control Congress, but delivering cheaper everyday life will require cooperation, difficult budget decisions and, in several areas, changes in policies still controlled by President Trump.
What to Watch Next

The first priorities will be Democrats' January 2027 legislative agenda, negotiations over Affordable Care Act subsidies and Medicaid, proposals to expand the Child Tax Credit, efforts to challenge import tariffs, congressional action concerning the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz, and any new measures targeting electricity and grocery costs. The response from President Trump and the possibility of bipartisan agreements will determine how much of the affordability agenda becomes law.
